l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: The ode celebrates Aristokleides of Aigina, who won a pankration victory at the Nemean games. It praises Aigina and Aiakos’ heroic lineage, recounting the deeds of Peleus, Telamon, Achilles, and other figures of that race. The poet asks the divine Muse to bring songs of triumph and declares that Aristokleides has brought new renown to Aigina through his victory at Nemea.

l: Aristokleides, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Aristokleides, son of Aristophanes, won a pankration victory at Nemea. Through his strength and fair deeds, he brought new renown to Aigina and earned praise from the poet.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Aigina is described as a Dorian isle crowded with strangers during the sacred festival of the Nemean games. It is identified as the ancient meeting-place of the Myrmidons and receives new glory through Aristokleides’ victory.

l: Muse, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: The divine Muse is asked to come to Aigina and provide songs of triumph. As the daughter of Zeus, she is invited to begin a noble lay to the king of heaven and to join it with singers’ voices and the lyre.

l: Nemean Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: The Nemean games are the sacred festival commemorated by the ode. Victory there is presented as deserving song, crowns, and praise.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: The pankration is the forceful contest in which Aristokleides competed. He did not disgrace the ancient meeting-place of the Myrmidons and won a victory described as a remedy for wearying blows.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Zeus is called the king of heaven, and the divine Muse is identified as his daughter. The blood of Aiakos’ race is also said to belong to Zeus, as do the games celebrated by the song.

l: Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Nemea is the deep-lying plain where Aristokleides won his victory. Its games, together with those of Epidauros and Megara, provide the occasion for his great renown.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Aiakos is the ancestor whose race the poet asks the Muse to praise. His lineage is presented as a fitting subject because its ancient valour provides glory close to home.

l: Aiakos' descendants, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Aiakos’ race is associated with a far-shining and enduring light. Its heroic members include Peleus, Telamon, and Achilles, and its blood is said to belong to Zeus.

l: Peleus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Peleus rejoiced when he cut his gigantic spear. He took Iolkos by his single arm without an army and held firm in his struggle with Thetis.

l: Thetis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Thetis is the daughter of the sea and was overcome or held firm by Peleus in struggle. She later became the mother of Achilles.

l: Telamon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Telamon helped sack the city of Laomedon while fighting beside Iolaos. He also followed Iolaos against the Amazons, and the terror of battle never weakened his courage.

l: Achilles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Achilles performed mighty deeds as a child while living in the house of Philyra. At six years old he killed lions and boars, hunted deer without dogs or nets, and later went to Troy, where he killed Memnon in battle.

l: Cheiron, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Cheiron reared Jason, Asklepios, and Achilles in his stone cavern. He taught Asklepios to prepare healing drugs and raised Achilles in a life of harmony until Achilles went to Troy.

l: Memnon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: Memnon was the chieftain of the Ethiops and a fiery cousin of Helenos. Achilles fought him hand to hand and determined that he would never return home.

l: victory at Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: The victory at Nemea belongs to Aristokleides, who achieved it in the pankration. It is celebrated as a source of honour for him, Aigina, and the Theoroi of the Pythian god.

l: song of triumph, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode III
s: The song of triumph is presented as the fitting companion of crowns and brave deeds. The poet asks the divine Muse for an abundant supply of it and offers Aristokleides a late gift of minstrelsy mingled with honey and white milk.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: The ode celebrates Timasarchos of Aigina as winner of the boys' wrestling-match at Nemea and praises his victories at several games. It invokes Zeus, Nemea, and the Aiakids, while recalling Timasarchos's deceased father Timokritos and the family's athletic honors. Much of the poem recounts the deeds and descendants of Herakles, Telamon, Peleus, and Thetis. It also praises Timasarchos's clan, his wreaths and renown, his uncle Kallikles, and his trainer Melesias.

l: Timasarchos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Timasarchos is celebrated as the winner of the boys' wrestling-match at Nemea. He has also won wreaths at the games of the Kleonaians, at Athens, and at seven-gated Thebes, and his clan's name is said to be preeminent in songs of victory.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Aigina is called the Aiakids' stronghold of goodly towers and the common light of all, aiding the stranger with justice. Timasarchos came from Aigina, and the Thebans honored his victory for Aigina's sake.

l: Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Nemea is invoked together with Zeus and Timasarchos's wrestling. The ode was sung for a victory won there.

l: boys' wrestling-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: The boys' wrestling-match is the contest in which Timasarchos won his victory at Nemea.

l: songs, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Songs, described as wise daughters of the Muses, comfort people and are more enduring than deeds when shaped by the Graces. They celebrate Timasarchos's victories and make a person's rare deeds comparable to those of kings.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Zeus the son of Kronos is invoked at the beginning of the hymn. He is also said to have ordained Peleus's destiny.

l: Timasarchos' father Timokritos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Timokritos is said to be dead, since he no longer sees the quickening sun. Had he been alive, he would have joined the ode with music and sung of his son's triumphs.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Herakles is associated with a splendid sepulchre at Thebes and with a fortunate hall where Timasarchos stayed as a friend. Together with Telamon, he destroyed Troy, the Meropes, and the warrior Alkyoneus.

l: Telamon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Telamon helped Herakles destroy Troy, the Meropes, and Alkyoneus. His descendants include Teukros, Aias, and the line of Achilles through his connection with the Aiakids.

l: Thetis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Thetis has power at Phthia and is described as one of the Nereids. She married Peleus, and their son was Neoptolemos.

l: Peleus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Peleus resisted the guileful counsels of Hippolyte and delivered Iolkos to the Haimones after confronting its troubles. Cheiron rescued him from an ambush, and he later married Thetis and received from the gods the prospect of a kingdom for himself and his seed.

l: Aiakids, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: The Aiakids are connected with Aigina, whose stronghold is praised as a common light and a just aid to strangers. The ode recounts the far-reaching lands and deeds of the sons of Aiakos.

l: Theandrid clan, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: The speaker came as a ready herald of athletic games for the Theandrid clan. Members of the clan competed at Olympia, Isthmos, and Nemea and returned home with wreaths whose fruitage was renown.

l: Nemean Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: The Nemean games are among the contests at which the Theandrid clan tested itself. Timasarchos won the boys' wrestling-match at Nemea.

l: wreaths, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Wreaths mark the victories of Timasarchos and the Theandrid clan. Timasarchos has won a chain of wreaths at the Kleonaians' games, Athens, and Thebes, while the clan returns from its contests with wreaths bringing renown.

l: song and poetic fame, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IV
s: Praise joined to music is said to comfort and to outlive a deed. Songs of victory give Timasarchos's clan renown, and praise of a person's rare deeds can make that person the peer of kings.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Nemean Ode V celebrates Pytheas of Aigina, son of Lampon, for winning the boys' pankration at Nemea. The ode praises Aigina, the Aiakidai, and Pytheas's maternal uncle Euthymenes, while briefly recounting the ancestry and legends of Aiakos, Phokos, Peleus, and Thetis. It also credits the Athenian trainer Menander and praises Themistios for victories in boxing and pankration at Epidauros.

l: Nemean Ode V, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Nemean Ode V celebrates Pytheas of Aigina, who won the boys' pankration at Nemea. It praises the Aiakidai and recounts parts of the stories of Aiakos, Phokos, Peleus, and Thetis.

l: Pytheas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Pytheas, son of Lampon, won the pankratiast's crown at Nemea while still too young to show the first down of manhood. He is a kinsman and successor of Euthymenes, and his trainer was Menander of Athens.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Aigina is Pytheas's mother-city and the place from which the ode's song is sent abroad. It is praised as a friendly field to strangers, famous for its ships, and the home of good men.

l: boys' pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: The boys' pankration was the contest in which Pytheas won at Nemea.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Pankration is the contest Pytheas won at Nemea. Themistios also won a double prize in boxing and pankration at Epidauros.

l: Nemean victory of Pytheas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Pytheas's Nemean victory brought honor to the Aiakidai and to Aigina. Nemea is described as favorable to him.

l: sweet song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: The sweet song refuses to be a statue standing idle on a pedestal; it travels from Aigina on trading ships and boats to spread news of Pytheas's victory.

l: Aiakidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: The Aiakidai are warrior heroes sprung from Kronos, Zeus, and the golden nymphs. Pytheas's victory honors them, and the ode recounts their ancestry and stories.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Zeus is named as the ancestor of the Aiakidai and as the grandsire whose altar stood on Aigina. Zeus Hellenios received the prayers of the Aiakidai for Aigina's good men and fame in shipping; Zeus also promised Peleus a sea-bride from among the Nereids.

l: Phokos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Phokos is described as the goddess-born royal strength, son of Aiakos and Psamatheia. He was killed by the sons of Endais, who then left the island.

l: Thetis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Thetis is a sea-bride from among the Nereids whom Zeus promised to find for Peleus, after persuading Poseidon. The Muses sang of her and Peleus at Pelion.

l: Peleus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Peleus is one of the glorious sons of Endais and a hero of the Aiakidai. Hippolyte falsely accused him of attempting to enter Akastos's bridal bed, but he refused her advances because he feared Zeus, the protector of hosts and guests; Zeus then promised him a sea-bride.

l: Euthymenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Euthymenes is Pytheas's maternal uncle and a kinsman of the same stock. He won hymns through a victory at Aigina, and he honors Pytheas by following in his footsteps.

l: Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Nemea is where Pytheas won the pankratiast's crown. It is described as favorable to Pytheas.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode V
s: Aiakos is the grandsire whose altar stood on Aigina, where his descendants prayed for the city's prosperity and fame. He is the father of Phokos, whom Psamatheia bore, and the husband of Endais.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: The ode celebrates Alkimidas of Aigina, winner of the boys' wrestling-match at Nemea. It praises his lineage, especially Praxidamas, and presents his victory as evidence that athletic distinction returns among successive generations. It also honors the Bassid clan and the Aiakidai by recalling their victories at Olympia, Isthmos, Nemea, and Pytho. Melesias is praised as the trainer who guided Alkimidas's hands and strength.

l: Alkimidas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: Alkimidas wins the boys' wrestling-match at Nemea and returns from the pleasant meeting-places of Nemea. His victory is presented as proof that his family, like fruitful fields, produces excellence in successive generations. The ode calls his victory the five-and-twentieth honor shown forth by his house and says that two Olympic wreaths were denied to him and Polytimidas by the fall of the lot.

l: Melesias, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: Melesias trains Alkimidas and guides his hands and strength as a charioteer guides a chariot. The ode compares him to a dolphin hurrying through the sea.

l: Praxidamas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: Praxidamas is Alkimidas's father and predecessor, whose footsteps Alkimidas follows. He won an Olympic olive-wreath for the Aiakidai, was crowned five times at Isthmos and three times at Nemea, and brought honor to Sokleides.

l: Bassid clan, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: The Bassid clan is described as an old and renowned race with abundant inherited material for song. The ode calls on the Muse to direct a gale of glorious song upon its house and celebrates its many athletic honors.

l: Aiakidai, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: The Aiakidai received an Olympic olive-wreath through Praxidamas. Their mighty feats have given chroniclers wide avenues of glory, and their name has spread over land, beyond the sea, and even to the Ethiopians through the story of Achilles's slaying of Memnon.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: Aigina is the place associated with Alkimidas's victory and with the Aiakidai. The ode may have been sung there at a feast of the Bassid clan in honor of the victory.

l: Nemea, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: Nemea is the site from which Alkimidas returns after winning the boys' wrestling-match. Praxidamas was crowned there three times, and parsley associated with the Nemean lion marked another victory by Kreontidas.

l: boys' wrestling-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: The boys' wrestling-match is won by Alkimidas. His success is described as following the ordinance of Zeus and as proving him a successful hunter in his wrestling quest.

l: Nemean Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: The Nemean Games are represented through the contests and crowns won at Nemea. Alkimidas wins there, while Praxidamas is said to have taken three Nemean crowns.

l: the ode, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: The ode honors Alkimidas's victory and praises the athletic achievements of his family and the Bassid clan. It recalls victories at Olympia, Isthmos, Nemea, and Pytho, and closes by praising Melesias's training of Alkimidas.

l: hereditary athletic excellence, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: Hereditary athletic excellence is illustrated by the comparison of Alkimidas's family with fruitful fields that yield and then gather strength. Alkimidas follows the athletic path of Praxidamas, while the family record includes distinguished athletes in alternating generations.

l: song and poetic fame, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VI
s: Poetic fame preserves noble deeds after people have vanished. The ode presents song as a means of carrying the Bassid clan's inherited renown forward and compares its own praise to an archer's accurate shot.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: The ode celebrates Sogenes of Aigina, son of Thearion, for winning the boys' pentathlon and praises his family and city. Pindar reflects on how song preserves great deeds, comparing the fame of Odysseus with the neglected excellence of Aias. He recounts the death and posthumous honors of Neoptolemos at Delphi and insists that he has not dishonored him. The poem concludes by invoking Zeus, Aiakos, and Herakles while praying for lasting prosperity for Sogenes, Thearion, and their descendants.

l: Destiny, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Fate assigns each person a separate lot and limits each to a different kind of life. It brings death equally to the famous and the obscure, and it required that one of the sons of Aiakos remain beside the sanctuary at Delphi.

l: Sogenes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Sogenes, son of Thearion, wins distinction in the boys' pentathlon and is celebrated as a victor from Aigina. Pindar praises his achievement, swears that he has not exceeded the proper bounds in praising him, and prays that Sogenes and his family may enjoy lasting strength, prosperity, and honor.

l: Thearion, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Thearion is the father of Sogenes and is praised for receiving a fair measure of happiness through courageous deeds, understanding, and sound judgment. Pindar declares himself Thearion's friend and prays for steadfast prosperity for him and his descendants.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Aigina is portrayed as a city of the spear-clashing sons of Aiakos that loves song and nurtures zeal for athletic competition. Pindar invokes Aigina while proclaiming the inherited path to glory of its children descended from Zeus.

l: The Pentathlon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: The pentathlon is the five-game athletic contest in which Sogenes wins the boys' prize. Its events are identified as the jump, discus throw, javelin throw, foot-race, and wrestling.

l: song and poetic fame, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Song preserves and rewards great deeds that would otherwise fall into darkness, with Mnemosyne enabling their remembrance through voice and verse. Pindar suggests that poetic song has made Odysseus' fame greater than his actual toils and can increase honor even for the dead.

l: death, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Death comes to the famous and the obscure alike. The text presents death as unavoidable, while noting that divine favor and honorable stories can preserve fame after death.

l: Odysseus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Odysseus' fame is said to have become greater than his toils through the sweet songs attributed to Homer. The persuasive excellence of those songs makes people accept his stories, even where they contain deception.

l: Homer, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Homer is credited with singing the sweet lays that enlarged Odysseus' fame. His poetic skill persuades listeners to accept the stories he tells.

l: Aias, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Aias is described as second only to Achilles in battle among the Greeks who went to Troy. Because people lacked true understanding, he struck himself through the midriff with a sword in anger over the arms.

l: Neoptolemos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Neoptolemos, son of Achilles, helped sack Priam's city and later became king for a short time in Molossia, whose kingdom his descendants continued to hold. He went to Delphi with spoils from Troy and was killed there by a man in a quarrel over meat; afterward he remained at Delphi as a heroic guardian of justice. Pindar repeatedly insists that he has not dishonored Neoptolemos with irretrievable words.

l: Trojan War, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: The Trojan War is represented through the Greek expedition to Ilos, the recovery of Menelaos' bride, and the sack of Priam's city. Neoptolemos participated in the war and carried spoils from Troy to Delphi.

l: Pytho, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Pytho is the place beneath whose floor Neoptolemos is said to lie. It is also associated with the ancient sanctuary where he remained after death.

l: Delphi, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Delphi is described as the god's home and as the place where Neoptolemos was killed after bringing spoils from Troy. Although the Delphian entertainers were deeply grieved, Neoptolemos remained there as one of the sons of Aiakos who watched over justice during sacrificial processions and games.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Aiakos is the ancestor of the sons who rule and gain glory in Aigina. Zeus begat him by a mortal mother, and he became ruler of cities in his own fortunate land.

l: Aiakids, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: The sons of Aiakos are associated with Aigina's inherited path to glory and with valorous deeds. One of them, Neoptolemos, is destined to remain at Delphi, where he oversees justice in connection with the heroes and the games.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Zeus is invoked when Nemea is named and is celebrated as the king of the gods. He is said to have fathered Aiakos by a mortal mother and to have made him ruler of cities.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VII
s: Herakles is called a loving friend and brother of Aiakos and is invoked alongside Zeus and Athene. Sogenes is described as wishing to live happily in the sacred street of his ancestors in a close bond with Herakles, whose favor can give mortals strength against difficulties.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Nemean Ode VIII celebrates Deinis of Aigina, winner of the short foot-race, and honors his father Meges and their clan. It invokes Aiakos and recalls the union of Zeus and Aigina, from which Aiakos was born to rule Oinone. The ode contrasts honorable virtue with envy, treacherous speech, and slander through the story of Aias and Odysseus. It presents song as a means of praising achievement, preserving reputation, and making labor painless.

l: Nemean Ode VIII, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Nemean Ode VIII celebrates Deinis of Aigina, winner of the short foot-race, and honors his father Meges. It invokes Aiakos and praises the enduring value of virtue, friendship, and song.

l: Deinis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Deinis is celebrated as the winner of the short foot-race. The ode bears a Lydian crown of song from Nemea for two races run by Deinis and his father Meges.

l: Meges, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Meges is Deinis's father and is honored alongside him for the two races. The speaker says that he cannot bring Meges's spirit back to earth but can raise a lofty column of song for his house and the clan of Chariadai.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Aigina is the beloved city and island associated with the ode. She was the mother of Aiakos through her union with Zeus, and the speaker seeks favor for her citizens.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Aiakos was born from Zeus and Aigina and became king of Oinone. The speaker clasps Aiakos's holy knees as a suppliant for Aigina and its citizens.

l: Stadion race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: The short foot-race was won by Deinis. The ode celebrates the glory from Nemea associated with two races run by Deinis and Meges.

l: envy, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Envy fastens on what is good and does not strive against what is base. The speaker connects envy with harmful speech and says that envy helped bring about Aias's destruction.

l: Aias, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Aias, the son of Telamon, was slain with his own sword after the Danaoi secretly awarded the golden arms to Odysseus. The ode says that Aias and Odysseus had both fought powerfully to defend the body of Achilles and in other labors.

l: Odysseus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Odysseus received the golden arms when the Danaoi secretly cast their votes in his favor. The ode presents this decision as part of the strife that led to Aias's death.

l: treacherous speech and slander, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Treacherous speech and slander are described as hateful, deceitful forces that twist stories, injure what shines, and raise the fame of obscure or unworthy people. The speaker rejects such paths and asks Zeus to let him follow simplicity.

l: virtue, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Virtue grows greater when wise and just people uphold it. The ode compares its growth to that of a tree rising toward the moist air after being watered by fresh dew.

l: song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode VIII
s: Song preserves honor by raising a lofty column of praise for Deinis, Meges, and their house. It can make labor painless, celebrate worthy deeds, and give the dead an honorable name among their children and townsfolk.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Nemean Ode IX celebrates Chromios of Aitna for winning a chariot race at the Pythian games at Sikyon. The song leads the triumph from Apollo at Sikyon to the newly founded city of Aitna and praises Chromios's wealth, courage, military service, and divine good fortune. It recalls Adrastos's foundation of the contest and the disastrous expedition of Amphiaraos and the other heroes against Thebes. The ode ends by renewing the victory through song, wine, and the honor bestowed by the Muses and the Charites.

l: Nemean Ode IX, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Nemean Ode IX celebrates Chromios of Aitna, winner in the chariot-race. Although placed among the Nemeans by usage, it concerns a victory won at Sikyon in the local Pythian games.

l: Chromios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Chromios is praised as the winner of a chariot-race at Sikyon and as a fortunate man of wealth, renown, courage, and military ability. The song says that he served in foot, horse, and naval fighting and helped ward off the destruction of Enyalios.

l: Aitna city, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Aitna is the new-made city to which the triumph is led from Sikyon. The song asks Zeus to grant its people good laws, long-lasting prosperity, and a share in the glories won by its citizens.

l: Sikyon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Sikyon is the place where Chromios won his chariot-race victory. The ode leads the triumph from Apollo at Sikyon toward Aitna and recalls the sacred crowns sent from Sikyon.

l: Apollo, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Apollo is associated with Sikyon and with the crowns awarded for Chromios's victory. The song honors Apollo and Leto's twin children, who keep watch over Pytho.

l: Muses, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: The Muses are called upon to lead the triumph to Aitna and to provide a song of sweetness for Chromios. The speaker claims, with their aid, to have cast his poetic javelin nearest to their mark.

l: the Pythian games at Sikyon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: The Pythian games at Sikyon are the local games in which Chromios won his chariot-race. The contest is identified as the event celebrated by the ode.

l: Chromios's chariot-race victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Chromios's chariot-race victory was won at Sikyon and is treated as the very crown of contests of steeds. Its crowns and prizes inspire the triumphal song, banquet, and celebration.

l: the triumphal procession to Aitna, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: The triumphal procession to Aitna carries the celebration from Apollo at Sikyon to the new city. It is directed toward Chromios's house, whose doors are opened to welcome visiting guests.

l: Adrastos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Adrastos ordained the contest beside the stream of Asopos in honor of Phoibos. As king in that place, he founded a new festival and athletic and chariot contests that made his city known and glorious.

l: Amphiaraos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Amphiaraos fled Argos with Adrastos before civil strife and later joined the expedition against seven-gated Thebes. Zeus opened the earth with a thunderbolt and buried Amphiaraos with his horses before Periklymenos could strike him from behind.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Zeus did not speed the expedition against Thebes, but warned the warriors through flashing lightning to halt their journey. He later buried Amphiaraos and his horses by splitting the deep-breasted earth with a thunderbolt, and the speaker asks Zeus to grant Aitna good laws and lasting prosperity.

l: the victory song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: The victory song is presented as the proper public record of a good deed and as a means of renewing a victory beside the banquet bowl. It praises Chromios's achievement with lyre, flute, voice, wine, and the favor of the Charites.

l: glory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode IX
s: Honor and glory arise from brave deeds, divine song, military courage, civic achievement, and athletic victory. The ode says that glory won together with great wealth gives a mortal no higher mountain-top to reach, while lust for gain can secretly steal the spirit of honor.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: The ode celebrates Theaios of Argos, winner of the wrestling-match at the Hekatombaia at Argos. It praises Argos, Hera's city, through its heroes, gods, women, and many athletic victories. Theaios is credited with victories at Pytho, the Isthmos, Nemea, the Gates of the Sea, the plains of Adrastos, and the festival of the Athenians. The closing myth recounts how Kastor was killed by Idas, how Polydeukes avenged him, and how Polydeukes chose to share immortality with his brother.

l: Theaios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Theaios, son of Oulias, won the wrestling-match twice at the Hekatombaia and thereby gained relief from his labors. He was also first at Pytho, won crowns at the Isthmos and Nemea, prevailed three times at the Gates of the Sea and three times on the plains of Adrastos, and twice won at the festival of the Athenians.

l: Hekatombaia at Argos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: The Hekatombaia at Argos was the festival at which Theaios won his wrestling victory. Its contests included a struggle for the bronze shield and sacrifices of oxen to Hera.

l: wrestling-match, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: The wrestling-match was won twice by Theaios, son of Oulias, at the Hekatombaia.

l: Argos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Argos is described as the city of Danaos and his fifty daughters, the home of Hera, and a fitting dwelling of gods. It is praised for the excellence of its men, heroes, women, athletic successes, and association with Perseus, Epaphos, Hypermnestra, Diomedes, Amphiaraos, Amphitryon, and Herakles.

l: Lynkeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Lynkeus, watching from Taygetos, saw Kastor and Polydeukes sitting within a hollow oak because he had the keenest eyes among men. He fought Polydeukes beside his father's sepulchre and was killed when Polydeukes drove a bronze spear into his side.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Herakles was born from Zeus's union with Alkmene after Zeus entered Amphitryon's hall in Amphitryon's likeness. Herakles became a bridegroom of Hebe in Olympos, and his ordinance at Pisa is identified with the Olympic games.

l: Hera, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Hera is associated with Argos, which is called her home. The Hekatombaia included sacrifices to Hera, and Hebe, Herakles' bride, is described as walking beside her mother, the queen of marriage.

l: Olympic games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: The Olympic games are called the ordinance of Herakles held at Pisa. Theaios and other competitors recognize their supremacy among the games.

l: Kastor, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Kastor was the brother of Polydeukes and was nominally a son of Tyndareus. Idas struck him with a bronze spear after Lynkeus discovered the brothers, and Kastor died with the death-gasp in his throat before Polydeukes appealed to Zeus.

l: Polydeukes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Polydeukes fought Idas and Lynkeus after Kastor was struck, killing Lynkeus with his spear while Zeus killed Idas with a thunderbolt. When Kastor lay dying, Polydeukes begged Zeus to let him die with his brother and chose to share life and death with him rather than remain wholly immortal in Olympos.

l: Idas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Idas, angered over oxen, struck Kastor with a bronze spear. He later faced Polydeukes beside his father's sepulchre and was killed by a thunderbolt from Zeus.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Zeus fathered Polydeukes and entered Alkmene's hall in the likeness of Amphitryon. He killed Idas with a thunderbolt and offered Polydeukes the choice between dwelling wholly in Olympos or sharing equal time with Kastor beneath the earth and in heaven.

l: Argive athletic victories, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Argos is celebrated for numerous athletic victories, including those of Theaios at Pytho, the Isthmos, Nemea, the Gates of the Sea, the plains of Adrastos, and the festival of the Athenians. The city's champions also won prizes at Corinth, among the men of Kleonai, at Sikyon, Pellene, Kleitor, Tegea, among the Achaians' cities, and at Lykaion.

l: death of Kastor, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Kastor was killed when Idas, angered over oxen, struck him with a bronze spear after Lynkeus saw the brothers in a hollow oak. Polydeukes found him not quite dead and appealed to Zeus for permission to share his brother's fate.

l: choice of Polydeukes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Polydeukes rejected the exclusive possibility of living in Olympos without death or old age. He chose instead to share equal time with Kastor, being alive beneath the earth for half the time and in the golden house of heaven for the other half.

l: shared immortality of Kastor and Polydeukes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode X
s: Kastor and Polydeukes received a shared existence through Polydeukes' choice. They dwell on alternate days with Zeus and in the hidden places beneath the earth at Therapnai, fulfilling an equal fate.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: The ode celebrates Aristagoras of Tenedos on his election as Prytanis, apparently the President of the Senate. It welcomes Aristagoras and his fellow senators to Hestia's sanctuary during the initiatory ceremonies and prays that he complete his twelve-month term with fair fame and an untroubled heart. Aristagoras is praised for his bodily excellence, courage, ancestry, and sixteen neighboring athletic victories in wrestling and the pankration. The ode also reflects on mortal uncertainty, warning against both excessive boasting and excessive mistrust of one's abilities.

l: Aristagoras of Tenedos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: Aristagoras is welcomed to Hestia's sanctuary on his election as Prytanis and is prayed to complete his twelve-month term with fair fame and an unvexed heart. He is praised for his splendid body, dauntless heart, noble ancestry, and sixteen victories in wrestling and the pankration among neighboring peoples. The ode says that excessive parental caution kept him from competing at the Pythian or Olympic contests, though the poet believes he would have won great honor there.

l: Tenedos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: Tenedos is kept in her place erect by Aristagoras and his fellow senators as they honor Hestia through drink-offerings, burnt sacrifices, music, songs, and the rites of Zeus, the stranger's friend.

l: Prytanis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: The Prytanis is presented as a kind of President of the Senate. Aristagoras assumes this office for a twelve-month term.

l: Senate of Tenedos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: The Senate is represented by Aristagoras and his fellows, who draw near to Hestia's glorious sceptre during the initiatory ceremonies and honor her through sacrifices, music, songs, and ritual feasts.

l: election of the Prytanis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: The election of the Prytanis occasions the ode for Aristagoras of Tenedos. His election is followed by initiatory ceremonies at which he is welcomed to Hestia's sanctuary.

l: initiatory ceremonies, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: The initiatory ceremonies accompany the election of a new Prytanis of Tenedos. During them, Aristagoras and his fellow senators approach Hestia's sanctuary and honor her with offerings, sacrifices, music, songs, and celebrations of Zeus's rites.

l: Hestia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: Hestia is addressed as the daughter of Rhea, sister of highest Zeus, and sharer of Hera's throne. She is asked to welcome Aristagoras and his fellow senators to her sanctuary, and she is honored as the guardian of the city halls through drink-offerings, burnt sacrifices, music, songs, and ritual feasts.

l: sixteen neighboring athletic victories, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Nemean Ode XI
s: Sixteen illustrious victories among neighboring peoples have crowned Aristagoras and his famous clan in wrestling and in the pankration. These victories are presented as evidence of his strength and athletic distinction.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, THE ISTHMIAN ODES.
s: The unit is titled “THE ISTHMIAN ODES.” It identifies the subject as The Isthmian Odes. No further information is provided about the work or its contents.

l: The Isthmian Odes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, THE ISTHMIAN ODES.
s: The Isthmian Odes are identified as the subject of this unit. No additional information about them is provided.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Pindar sets aside an intended song for Apollo at Delos in order to celebrate Herodotos of Thebes and his chariot victory. He praises Thebes, noting that Isthmus has granted its people six crowns, and compares Herodotos’ driving with the legendary chariot skills of Kastor and Iolaos. The ode also honors Herodotos’ father Asopodoros and his new home Orchomenos, which sheltered him after a shipwreck. Pindar prays that Herodotos will win further victories at Pytho, Alpheos, and Olympia and bring honor to seven-gated Thebes.

l: Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Pindar postpones a song intended for Apollo at Delos in order first to praise Herodotos of Thebes and his victory. He celebrates Herodotos, his father Asopodoros, Thebes, Isthmus, and the prospect of Herodotos winning further crowns.

l: Herodotos of Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Herodotos is honored for winning a chariot race with his four-horsed car while handling the reins himself, without assistance. He is praised as one who may yet win wreaths from Pytho, Alpheos, and the Olympian games and bring honor to Thebes.

l: Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Thebes is addressed as Pindar’s mother and as a city whose interests take precedence over the song intended for Delos. It is praised as the home of Herodotos and as seven-gated Thebes, whose honor Herodotos is expected to increase.

l: Delos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Delos is the rocky Apollonian island to which Pindar is vowed and for which he had intended to compose a song. Pindar asks it to make room while he joins that future song with the present celebration.

l: Isthmos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Isthmus is praised as the place that has given the people of Kadmos six crowns in its games. Pindar invokes Poseidon and holy Isthmus while celebrating Herodotos’ victory.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: The Isthmian Games are associated with six crowns won by the people of Kadmos, bringing glory to Thebes. Their victories are treated as a fair distinction for Herodotos’ native country.

l: chariot race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: The chariot race is the contest in which Herodotos wins, driving his four-horsed car himself. Pindar presents the victory as worthy of praise and links it with the celebrated chariot skill of Kastor and Iolaos.

l: Herodotos' four-horsed car, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Herodotos’ four-horsed car is honored in song for its victory. Herodotos handles its reins with no helping hand, and Pindar attributes its speed to Poseidon.

l: Asopodoros, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Asopodoros is identified as Herodotos’ father. Pindar promises to honor the story of his fate, including his being driven ashore by a wrecked ship and later rising again to enjoy better fortune.

l: Orchomenos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Orchomenos is described as Asopodoros’ new country. It sheltered him after he was driven ashore from a wrecked ship and is included among the places whose glory Pindar will celebrate.

l: Mortal excellence, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Valour is presented as worthy of high praise when a person pursues it through wealth and toil and succeeds. Those who achieve it deserve generous public recognition in words.

l: glory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode I
s: Fame is described as a valuable reward for victory in games or war, greater than the rewards sought by ordinary workers merely to escape hunger. The text warns that a person who hides wealth and mocks others may die without having known good fame.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The unit contains a footnote identifying the Pentathlon. It refers the reader to the Introduction to Ol. xiii and the note on Nem. vii, p. 129. No further information about the Pentathlon is provided here.

l: The Pentathlon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, notes
s: The Pentathlon is identified in a footnote, which directs the reader to the Introduction to Ol. xiii and the note on Nem. vii, p. 129 for further information.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode II
s: The ode honors Xenokrates of Akragas for winning the Isthmian chariot-race and other victories at Krisa, Athens, and Olympia. It is addressed to Thrasyboulos, Xenokrates' son, and urges him not to remain silent about his father's achievements. Xenokrates is praised as a distinguished citizen, supporter of horse-racing, worshipper at festivals, and generous host. Nikesippos is instructed to deliver this message to Thrasyboulos.

l: Xenokrates of Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode II
s: Xenokrates won the Isthmian chariot-race, for which Poseidon gave him a Dorian parsley wreath. He also gained glory at Krisa, Athens, and Olympia, and is praised as a distinguished citizen of Akragas, supporter of horse-racing, worshipper at festivals, and generous host.

l: Thrasyboulos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode II
s: Thrasyboulos is identified as Xenokrates' son and is addressed as the recipient of the ode's praise. He is urged not to remain silent about his father's prowess, and Nikesippos is told to deliver that message to him.

l: Akragas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode II
s: Akragas is the community whose people are associated with Xenokrates, who is called a light of its people.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode II
s: The Isthmian victory celebrated in the ode was won by Xenokrates in a chariot-race. Poseidon is said to have granted him this victory and its Dorian parsley wreath.

l: chariot-race, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode II
s: Xenokrates won the chariot-race at the Isthmian Games. His chariot and the driving of the horses are praised, including the skill of Nikomachos, who managed the reins at Athens.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Isthmian Ode III celebrates Melissos of Thebes, winner in the pankration and a victor in the chariot-race at Nemea. It praises the Kleonymid clan's ancient athletic fame, its losses in war, and the revival of its glory through Melissos. Melissos's small stature is contrasted with his courage and skill, especially through comparison with Herakles's wrestling match against the giant Antaios. The ode also honors Herakles and describes the sacrifices and yearly games held at Thebes.

l: Isthmian Ode III, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Isthmian Ode III celebrates Melissos of Thebes after his victories in the pankration and chariot-race. It praises the Kleonymid clan, invokes Herakles, and presents athletic success as a renewal of the clan's ancient glory.

l: Melissos of Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Melissos wins crowns at the Isthmian games and in the chariot-race at Nemea, proclaiming Thebes as his home. Despite his small and unimpressive stature, he is formidable in strength, courage, and wrestling skill, and he wins a double victory at the yearly games after an earlier victory among the boys.

l: Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Thebes is the home of Melissos and the Kleonymidai. The city prepares a feast and new-built altar-ring for Herakles on the heights Elektrai and holds yearly games there.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: The pankration is the contest in which Melissos wins his Isthmian victory. His success in it becomes the subject of a song comparing his methods with those of Herakles against Antaios.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: At the Isthmian games Melissos wins a crown in the pankration. His victory gives the poet a means to celebrate the excellence and renewed fame of the Kleonymid clan.

l: Nemean chariot victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Melissos wins a chariot-race in the hollow vale of the deep-chested lion, identified in the ode with Nemea. This victory, together with his Isthmian crown, gives him two prizes and allows him to proclaim Thebes as his home.

l: Kleonymid clan, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: The Kleonymid clan has ancient fame in chariot racing and is related on the mother's side to the Labdakidai. Four members of the house are lost in a single day of war, but the clan's glory blossoms again through Melissos's victories.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Zeus is the source of all high excellence among mortals. Those who honor him may enjoy lasting happiness, while prosperity does not remain steadfast with perverse minds.

l: Poseidon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Poseidon, called the Shaker of Earth and associated with Onchestos and the Isthmus, gives the Kleonymid house the hymn of wonder. He leads its ancient glory out of sleep and causes it to shine again.

l: Isthmos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: The Isthmus is described as the bridge between the seas before the valley of Corinth. Its games provide Melissos with one of the two crowns celebrated in the ode.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Herakles is praised as the son of Alkmene who traveled across the earth and sea, made safe passage for ships, and overcame Antaios. He now dwells beside the aegis-bearer, is honored by the immortals, has Hebe as his wife, and receives sacrifices and games at Thebes.

l: Antaios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Antaios is a giant in Libya who wrestles against Herakles. He had been roofing Poseidon's temple with the skulls of strangers until Herakles, though short in stature, came from Kadmean Thebes and defeated him.

l: Herakles's wrestling match with Antaios, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Herakles's match with Antaios serves as a comparison for Melissos's contest. Both Herakles and Melissos are presented as men of small stature whose courage, strength, and skill overcome larger or formidable opponents.

l: Mortal excellence, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Mortal excellence comes from Zeus and is subject to changing fortune. The ode says that even the better man may be overtaken by a worse through craft, while noble deeds can preserve a person's reputation beyond mortal life.

l: glory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: Glory and fame arise from brave deeds and skillful song. The ode presents poetic praise as a beacon whose light can shine over the earth and sea and preserve excellence for all time.

l: chariot, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode III
s: The chariot is central to the Kleonymid clan's inherited athletic reputation. Kleonymos and his descendants compete with the curved chariot in major Greek contests, spend wealth on horses, and win victories at Athens, Sikyon, and Nemea.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Isthmian Ode IV celebrates Phylakidas of Aigina for winning the pankration and praises his brother Pytheas, who helped guide his training. The ode invokes Theia and reflects on wealth, success, fame, and the divine source of human strength. It honors Aigina and the sons of Aiakos, recalling their heroic deeds and Aigina’s seamen’s role in the deliverance of Salamis during the battle of Salamis. The poem concludes by calling for a crown, a fillet, and a new song to celebrate Phylakidas’s victory.

l: Isthmian Ode IV, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Isthmian Ode IV was written for Phylakidas of Aigina, winner in the pankration. It praises Phylakidas, Pytheas, Aigina, the sons of Aiakos, and the honor gained through games and heroic deeds.

l: Phylakidas of Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Phylakidas is celebrated as the winner of the pankration. He receives praise for his strength and victory, including a double glory at Isthmos and a pankratiast’s crown at Nemea.

l: Pytheas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Pytheas is identified as Phylakidas’s brother and is also praised as a pankratiast. He guided Phylakidas’s blows in the struggle and helped him defeat a cunning opponent.

l: Theia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Theia is invoked as the mother of the Sun and as a goddess of many names. Men prize gold and honor through her influence.

l: wealth, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Wealth is described as containing two things that make life especially sweet: good success and the fair fame that follows it. Gold is praised as mighty above all else, and wealth is associated with the honor of Theia.

l: games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Games bring longed-for glory to those whose strong hands or swift feet win wreaths. The ode presents victory in games as a source of honor and celebrates Phylakidas’s success in them.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: The pankration is the contest in which Phylakidas won. Pytheas is praised for guiding Phylakidas in this struggle of hands that brings opponents low.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: The Isthmian Games are represented through Phylakidas’s double glory stored at Isthmos. His success there forms part of the honor celebrated in the ode.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Aigina is praised as the commonwealth of equal laws and as an island whose high-adventuring valour has been honored from long ago. Its sons, especially the sons of Aiakos, provide many subjects for song, and its seamen helped deliver Salamis.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Zeus is said to approve the might of men and to grant or order human outcomes. He is also called lord of all, and his grace gives poets material for praising great warriors.

l: Aiakids, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: The sons of Aiakos are central to the poet’s song about Aigina. They twice sacked the Trojans’ town, first with Herakles and later with the sons of Atreus, and are honored in Oinone.

l: Salamis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Salamis, called Aias’s city, could bear witness to Aigina’s seamen helping deliver it during a destructive tempest of Zeus. The event is recalled as a feat of Aiginetan valor, though the ode warns against boasting.

l: battle of Salamis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: The battle of Salamis is recalled through the deliverance of Salamis by Aigina’s seamen amid heavy destruction and widespread death. The ode attributes the ordering of such events to Zeus.

l: song, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Song preserves the honor of great warriors and gives lasting glory through the lute, pipe, and the work of poets. The ode itself is a new winged hymn intended to celebrate Phylakidas’s victory.

l: glory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Glory comes through success in games, fair fame, heroic deeds, and their telling in song. Phylakidas receives glory at Isthmos and Nemea, while Aigina’s heroes gain enduring glory through poetry and worship.

l: victory, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode IV
s: Victory is celebrated as the result of successful effort in games and as a source of honor. Phylakidas’s pankration victory is marked with a crown, a fleecy fillet, and a new hymn.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: The ode honors Phylakidas of Aigina, who has won the pankration at the Isthmian Games, and celebrates his family’s athletic victories. It praises Lampon, Phylakidas’s father, for cultivating excellence, hospitality, moderation, and a consistent character. The poem recalls Herakles’ expedition with Telamon, the birth and naming of Aias, and the heroic fame of Aiakos’ descendants. It concludes with the poet offering Lampon a drink of song from the sacred spring of Dirke.

l: Phylakidas of Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Phylakidas, the youngest son of Lampon, won the pankration at the Isthmian Games. His victory is the occasion for the ode, which also celebrates his family’s athletic achievements.

l: Lampon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Lampon is the father of Phylakidas and is praised for practicing whatever he undertakes, honoring Hesiod’s teaching, encouraging his sons, welcoming strangers, and pursuing the just mean. His speech is said to agree with his thoughts, and among athletes he is compared to a Naxian whetstone that sharpens others.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Aigina is honored through the song and is described as a city loved by the gods. The poet makes a libation of honey-speaking song in her honor.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Phylakidas won the pankration at the Isthmian Games. The family is also said to have gained three victories in the pankration at Isthmos, along with victories at Nemea.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: The Isthmian Games provided the occasion for Phylakidas’s victory in the pankration. The ode also records three pankration victories at Isthmos by the noble sons and their mother’s brother.

l: Nemean Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: The family won victories at leafy Nemea, and the poet recalls that the first libation was made to Zeus when a Nemean crown was won.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: The first libation was made to Zeus after victory at Nemea, and a third is planned for Zeus the Saviour and the Olympic god. Zeus answered Herakles’ prayer by sending a mighty eagle and granting Telamon a brave son.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Aiakos is identified as the father of Telamon and as the ancestor of the heroic line celebrated in the ode. His descendants are praised for their widespread fame.

l: Aiakos' descendants, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: The golden-charioted descendants of Aiakos are said to possess fame that travels along innumerable roads beyond Egypt and among the Hyperboreans. Their line includes Peleus, Telamon, and Aias, whose deeds are known even among peoples of unfamiliar speech.

l: Telamon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Telamon accompanied Herakles to Troy and helped him kill the Meropes and Alkyoneus. During a feast, Telamon challenged Herakles to make the opening libation and received Herakles’ prayer for a brave son.

l: Aias, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Aias was born to Telamon from Eriboia’s womb after Herakles prayed to Zeus for a son as strong in body and spirit as the lion skin he wore. Herakles named him after the eagle sent by Zeus and foretold that he would be formidable in battle.

l: Herakles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Herakles took Telamon and the Tirynthians by ship to Troy to avenge Laomedon’s falsehood. He captured Pergamos, killed the Meropes and the giant herdsman Alkyoneus, prayed for Telamon’s son, and received Zeus’s sign through the eagle.

l: Pytheas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: Pytheas is named with Phylakidas and Euthymenes as part of the family whose victories the poet celebrates. He is also identified as the athlete associated with the earlier Nemean victory.

l: Muses, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: The poet calls on the Muses’ melody to honor Lampon’s athletic progeny. He asks the Muse to serve as a dispenser of triumphal songs for Phylakidas, Pytheas, and Euthymenes.

l: song of triumph, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode V
s: The poet presents the ode as a triumphal song for Phylakidas and his family. He finally offers Lampon the sacred water of Dirke, symbolically giving him song made by the daughters of Mnemosyne.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: The ode celebrates Strepsiades of Thebes, winner of the pankration at Isthmos. It recalls Thebes’ mythic deeds and says that its ancient glory sleeps unless song preserves it. Strepsiades shares his crown with his uncle, who died fighting in war while defending his country. The poem ends by asking Loxias to grant another crown at the Pythian games and warns against aspiring beyond mortal limits through the example of Bellerophon.

l: Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: Thebes is praised for its mythic associations, including the births of Dionysos and Herakles, the wisdom of Teiresias, Iolaos, the Spartoi, the defeat of Adrastos, and the deeds of the Dorian colony and the sons of Aigeus. Its ancient glory is said to sleep because mortals are forgetful of it.

l: Strepsiades of Thebes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: Strepsiades wins the pankration prize at Isthmos. He is described as remarkably strong, handsome, and courageous, and he gives his uncle of the same name a share in his crown.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: The pankration is the contest in which Strepsiades wins a prize at Isthmos.

l: Isthmos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: At Isthmos, Strepsiades carries away the pankratiast’s prize.

l: Strepsiades's uncle, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: Strepsiades’s uncle, also named Strepsiades and identified as the son of Diodotos, dies after bronze-shielded Ares gives him over to death in battle. He is praised alongside Meleagros, Hektor, and Amphiaraos for fighting at the front, and his renown remains as a recompense for his valor.

l: song and poetic fame, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: Song preserves the glory of the past for mortals who attain the full reward granted by the wisdom of bards. The poet now leads Strepsiades’s new triumph in a melodious hymn and says that he will sing after receiving calm following sorrow.

l: war, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: War is portrayed as a cloud from which a warrior wards off a bloody shower while destroying the enemy host. A warrior who defends his country increases the renown of his fellow citizens even after death.

l: Poseidon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VI
s: Poseidon, called the earth-grasper, grants the speaker calm after a storm of grief. The poem also asks Loxias, rather than Poseidon, for a new crown at the Pythian games.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: The ode celebrates Kleandros of Aigina for winning the pankration at the Isthmian Games and for showing strength at Nemea. It is meant to be sung before the house of his father, Telesarchos, and urges young men to honor Kleandros with song and a myrtle wreath. The poet connects Aigina’s glory with Aiakos, Peleus, and Achilles, recounting how Themis’ oracle concerning Thetis’ son led to Thetis’ wedding with Peleus. The ode also praises Nikokles, Kleandros’ kinsman, for winning a boxing victory at the Isthmian Games, while celebrating the expulsion of the Persians and the return of freedom to Hellas.

l: Kleandros, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Kleandros of Aigina won the pankration at the Isthmian Games and showed his strength at the games of Nemea. The ode calls on young men to sing before the house of Telesarchos and to crown Kleandros with tender myrtle for his victory. He had also been successful at the games associated with Alkathoos and at the games of Epidauros.

l: Telesarchos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Telesarchos is identified as Kleandros’ father. His shining portal is the place before which the young men are urged to sing in honor of Kleandros.

l: Aigina, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Aigina is the island associated with Kleandros and the house of Telesarchos. The poet offers Aigina the choicest gift of the Graces and connects its glory with Aiakos, Achilles, and the Aiakid race.

l: pankration, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: The pankration is the contest in which Kleandros won his victory. Kleandros’ pankratiast victory is honored with a proposed wreath of tender myrtle.

l: Isthmian Games, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: The Isthmian Games provided Kleandros with a victory in the pankration. The Isthmian vale also witnessed Nikokles’ boxing victory, for which he won the Dorian parsley.

l: Persians, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: The Persians had been finally expelled before the ode was written. Their defeat ended the terror that had caused the poet’s disquietude.

l: expulsion of the Persians, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: The expulsion of the Persians brought an end to the terror that had hung over Hellas. The poet says that this relief permits people to set pleasant things before them despite earlier pain.

l: Hellas, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Hellas had been under an intolerable terror compared with a Tantalos-stone hanging above its head. The expulsion of the Persians removed that terror, and freedom is presented as enabling mortals to cure their troubles.

l: Zeus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Zeus favored Aigina and Thebe, the two daughters of Asopos. Zeus fathered Aiakos with Aigina, and Zeus was one of the gods who desired Thetis as a bride before hearing the oracle concerning her son.

l: Aiakos, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Aiakos was born to Zeus and Aigina and was regarded as the best of men upon the earth. Even among divinities he became a decider of strife, and his godlike sons and grandsons were foremost in battle.

l: Aiakos' descendants, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: The Aiakid race descended from Aiakos and included Achilles. Achilles glorified Aigina and the root from which he sprang through his victories in battle.

l: Poseidon, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Poseidon desired Thetis as a bride and contended with Zeus for her hand. The oracle warned that Thetis’ son would be mightier than his father and would wield a bolt more terrible than Poseidon’s dread trident.

l: Thetis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Thetis was a sea-goddess whose marriage was desired by Zeus and Poseidon. Themis declared that Thetis would bear a son mightier than his father, and Thetis was therefore directed to marry the mortal Peleus.

l: Themis, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Themis of wise counsels announced the oracle concerning the future son of Thetis. She advised that Thetis be given to Peleus so that her son would be born from a mortal marriage.

l: Peleus, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Peleus, son of Aiakos, was described as the most righteous according to human speech. Themis advised that Thetis be given to Peleus, and he became her mortal bridegroom.

l: Thetis' wedding, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Thetis’ wedding to Peleus was arranged after Themis’ oracle warned that a son of Thetis by Zeus or one of Zeus’ brothers would surpass his father. Zeus and Poseidon attended the wedding among the other guests.

l: Achilles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Achilles was the valorous son born from Thetis’ marriage to Peleus. He stained the plain of Mysia with the blood of Telephos, secured the return of the sons of Atreus, and killed or overcame champions including Memnon and Hektor at Troy. His funeral pyre and tomb were honored by the Helikonian maiden-choir, and his deeds glorified Aigina and the Aiakid race.

l: Troy, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Troy was defended by men whom Achilles overcame as he carried out slaughterous battle. Achilles cut through the strength of Troy’s defenders and led them toward the house of Persephone.

l: Nikokles, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: Nikokles was a boxer and a kinsman of Kleandros through Kleandros’ father’s noble brother. He won the Dorian parsley in the Isthmian vale, and the Muses’ chariot is said to proclaim his glory.

l: oracle concerning Thetis' son, The Extant Odes of Pindar, Isthmian Ode VII
s: The oracle concerning Thetis’ son foretold that Thetis would bear a royal offspring mightier than his father. The son would wield a bolt more terrible than lightning or Poseidon’s trident if Thetis married Zeus or one of Zeus’ brothers, so Themis advised that Thetis marry Peleus instead.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: The unit concerns the Fragments and their classification. Nearly two-thirds of the Fragments cannot be assigned to any distinct class. The remaining Fragments are divided among ten classes, including Epinikia, Hymnoi, Paianes, Dithyramboi, Prosodia, Parthenia, Hyporchaemata, Enkomia, Skolia, and Thraenoi. These classes comprise various types of odes, hymns, processional songs, dance songs, banquet songs, and dirges.

l: Fragments, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Nearly two-thirds of the Fragments cannot be assigned to any distinct class. The remainder is divided among ten classes of songs and odes.

l: distinct classes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Nearly two-thirds of the Fragments cannot be assigned to any distinct class. The remaining Fragments are divided among ten distinct classes.

l: Epinikia (Triumphal Odes), The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Epinikia are Triumphal Odes, such as the odes remaining to us entire.

l: Hymnoi (Hymns), The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Hymnoi are hymns sung by a choir in honour of gods.

l: Paianes, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Paianes are hymns of a kind like Hymnoi, but were anciently addressed especially to Apollo and Artemis for their intervention against pestilence.

l: Dithyramboi, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Dithyramboi are choral songs of more general compass that sometimes verge on the drama.

l: Prosodia (Processional Songs), The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Prosodia are Processional Songs.

l: Parthenia (Songs for a Choir of Maidens), The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Parthenia are songs for a choir of maidens.

l: Hyporchaemata (Songs with Accompaniment of Dance), The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Hyporchaemata are songs with accompaniment of dance.

l: Enkomia, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Enkomia are odes sung by a komos in praise of some person, but not necessarily on any special occasion.

l: Skolia (Songs to be sung at Banquets), The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Skolia are songs to be sung at banquets.

l: Thraenoi (Dirges), The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENTS.
s: Thraenoi are dirges.

l: The Extant Odes of Pindar, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENT OF A DITHYRAMB,
s: The singer (speaker) calls on the Olympian gods to dance at Athens and receive crowns and drink-offerings. The singer (speaker) has come from the house of Zeus to sing again for Bromios, the ivy-crowned god of clamorous shout, and to sing the offspring of the Highest and Kadmeän mothers. The unit describes spring at Argive Nemea, when violets and roses appear, flute-accompanied songs sound, and hymns honor Semele.

l: the blessed gods, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENT OF A DITHYRAMB,
s: The Olympian gods are invited to dance, descend with grace, glorify Athens, receive violet-entwined crowns and drink-offerings of spring-gathered herbs, and look on the singer (speaker).

l: Athens, The Extant Odes of Pindar, FRAGMENT OF A DITHYRAMB,
s: Athens is described as the city containing an incensed centre-stone and a famed market-place of splendid ornament. The Olympian gods are invited to visit it.
